docs.title: private_attribute_cpp
docs.text:
True C++-style private attributes for Python, enforced at the C level.

private_attribute is a C++ extension module that lets you declare attributes accessible only from inside the class that owns them — genuinely hidden from the outside world, from subclasses, and from hasattr(), dir(), and obj.__dict__.

Unlike Python's name-mangling (_Class__name) and the leading-underscore convention, these attributes cannot be reached at all from outside the declaring class's own code.

  • :material-lock: Enforced at the C level

    Attribute access is rewritten in tp_getattro / tp_setattro, not emulated in Python.

  • :material-eye-off: Truly hidden

    Not in __dict__. Invisible to hasattr(), getattr(), and dir().

  • :material-family-tree: Inheritance-safe

    Subclasses cannot see a parent's private state unless you explicitly opt in.

  • :material-package-variant: Zero dependencies

    A single compiled extension vendoring the header-only PicoSHA2 for hashing.

docs.title: A taste
docs.text:
from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class BankAccount(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_balance"]

    def __init__(self, balance):
        self._balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self._balance += amount       # ✅ accessible inside the class

    @property
    def balance(self):
        return self._balance

acct = BankAccount(100)
print(acct.balance)     # 100
acct.deposit(50)
print(acct.balance)     # 150

print(hasattr(acct, "_balance"))   # False — truly hidden
print(acct._balance)               # AttributeError: private attribute

Continue with the Quick Start or dive into the Guide.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Language C++17, CPython C-API Python ≥ 3.10 (CPython only, including free-threaded t builds) Platforms Linux, macOS, Windows License MIT

docs.title: PrivateAttrBase
docs.text:
class PrivateAttrBase(metaclass=PrivateAttrType):
    __slots__ = ()
    __private_attrs__ = ()

The base class to inherit from to create a class with private attributes. It has no special behavior on its own; all the machinery lives in its metaclass.

docs.title: PrivateAttrType
docs.text:
class PrivateAttrType(type):
    def __new__(cls, name, bases, attrs, /, *,
                private_func=None, use_parents=False): ...

The metaclass that implements private-attribute rewriting. You rarely use it directly unless you are building a custom metaclass.

docs.title: PrivateWrapProxy
docs.text:
class PrivateWrapProxy(Generic[_TVar, _T]):
    def __init__(self, decorator, orig=None, /): ...
    def __call__(self, func, /) -> _PrivateWrap[_T]: ...

A decorator that wraps an arbitrary decorator so it remains private-attribute-aware. See Decorated methods.

docs.title: _PrivateWrap
docs.text:
class _PrivateWrap(Generic[_T]):
    @property
    def result(self) -> _T: ...
    @property
    def funcs(self) -> _listproxy[FunctionType]: ...

The object returned by PrivateWrapProxy. It is transparent: __getattr__, __call__, and __get__ forward to .result.

docs.title: _listproxy
docs.text:
class _listproxy(Generic[_T]):
    def copy(self) -> list[_T]: ...
    def count(self, value, /) -> int: ...
    def index(self, value, start=0, stop=sys.maxsize, /) -> int: ...
    def __len__(self) -> int: ...
    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[_T]: ...
    def __getitem__(self, key) -> Any: ...
    def __contains__(self, value) -> bool: ...

A read-only proxy over a list. It is returned by _PrivateWrap.funcs and supports the common read-side list interface (len, iteration, indexing, in, copy, count, index) but has no mutating methods.

docs.title: prepare
docs.text:
def prepare(name, bases, attrs, /, **kwds) -> _PrivateTemp: ...

Context manager for building a private-attribute class inside a custom metaclass. Returns a temporary object exposing .name, .bases, .attrs, and .kwds (plus, since v2.1.17, a .postprocess(typ) shortcut).

docs.title: postprocess
docs.text:
def postprocess(typ, temp, /) -> None: ...

Finalizes a class created via prepare. Call it after the metaclass's own type.__new__.

docs.title: register_metaclass
docs.text:
def register_metaclass(typ, /) -> None: ...

Registers a custom metaclass so it can produce private-attribute classes. Must be called before creating any such class; the metaclass must support weakrefs.

docs.title: ensure_type
docs.text:
def ensure_type(typ, /) -> None: ...

Resets tp_getattro / tp_setattro / tp_finalizer slots on a type.

docs.title: ensure_metaclass
docs.text:
def ensure_metaclass(typ, /) -> None: ...

Resets the corresponding slots on a metaclass.

docs.title: Class-definition options
docs.text: Option Type Default Meaning __private_attrs__ str | Sequence[str] () The private attribute names. private_func (obj_id: int, attr_name: str) -> str None Custom hidden-name generator. use_parents bool False Merge ancestors' private names into this class's own set.

docs.title: Custom Metaclasses
docs.text: To combine private attributes with another metaclass (for example ABCMeta), use the prepare / postprocess pair and register the metaclass.

docs.title: Example: private attributes + ABC
docs.text:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod
import private_attribute

class PrivateAbcMeta(ABCMeta):
    def __new__(cls, name, bases, attrs, **kwargs):
        with private_attribute.prepare(name, bases, attrs, **kwargs) as temp:
            typ = super().__new__(cls, temp.name, temp.bases, temp.attrs, **temp.kwds)
            private_attribute.postprocess(typ, temp)   # or temp.postprocess(typ)
            return typ

private_attribute.register_metaclass(PrivateAbcMeta)

Now a class can behave as both an ABC and a private-attribute class:

class MyClass(metaclass=PrivateAbcMeta):
    __private_attrs__ = ("_a",)
    __slots__ = ()

    @abstractmethod
    def my_function(self): ...

class MyImplement(MyClass):
    __private_attrs__ = ("_a",)
    def __init__(self, value=1):
        self._a = value

    def my_function(self):
        return self._a

a = MyImplement(1)
a.my_function()          # 1
a._a                     # AttributeError: private attribute

MyClass()                # TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MyClass
                         # without an implementation for abstract method 'my_function'

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• prepare(name, bases, attrs, **kwds) is a context manager (since v2.2.3) that returns a temporary object holding .name, .bases, .attrs, and .kwds.
  • Call your metaclass's super().__new__ with those values, then finalize with postprocess(typ, temp) (or temp.postprocess(typ)).
  • register_metaclass tells the module about your metaclass so the private attribute machinery is installed correctly.

Locking

Since v2.2.1, prepare takes an internal creation lock so only one private-attribute type is being built (type.__new__) at a time. postprocess releases it. The lock is released automatically if construction fails. Prefer the with form (v2.2.3+) to guarantee release.

docs.title: ensure_type / ensure_metaclass
docs.text:
CPython may change tp_getattro / tp_setattro when you assign __getattribute__ / __setattr__. Use ensure_type (for types) or ensure_metaclass (for metaclasses) to reset those slots, and avoid setting those dunder methods on private-attribute classes directly.

private_attribute.ensure_type(SomeClass)
private_attribute.ensure_metaclass(SomeMeta)

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
The module is built with scikit-build-core and CMake. It vendors the header-only PicoSHA2 library for SHA-256 hashing, so there are no external C++ dependencies.

git clone https://github.com/Locked-chess-official/private_attribute_cpp.git

pip install .

To build a wheel instead:

pip install build
python -m build

Debug symbols

Set PRIVATE_ATTR_KEEP_DEBUG=1 to retain debug symbols in a Linux build (otherwise -g0 is applied by CMake). The CI test workflow sets this flag so native crash backtraces carry full symbols.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
• __private_attrs__ must be a string or a sequence of strings.
  • Names declared in __slots__ cannot also be in __private_attrs__; however, private attributes may still be set in methods even when __slots__ is defined (they live in private-attribute storage, not __dict__).
  • Instances of PrivateAttrBase (and its subclasses) are not picklable by default.
  • Private names are ultimately rewritten to a tuple of two hashes (unless a custom private_func is supplied).
  • _PrivateWrap objects are transparently unwrapped back to the original object during class creation.
  • Do not pass PrivateWrapProxy a decorator that itself returns a _PrivateWrap — this raises TypeError.
  • A class nested inside another class cannot use the outer class's private attributes.
  • If a parent class defines an attribute that is not in its __private_attrs__ (nor a PrivateAttrType instance), a child class must not list that name in its own __private_attrs__.

docs.title: Version changelog (behavioral)
docs.text: Version Change 2.1.0 Subclass code can no longer access a parent's private attributes; re-declaring the name stores it separately (instance attrs per declaring class, class attrs per class). 2.1.4 __private_attrs__ became optional. 2.1.17 _PrivateTemp gained a .postprocess(typ) shortcut. 2.2.0 Subclass must not define a parent-private name in its own body unless declared in its own __private_attrs__ or use_parents=True. use_parents added. 2.2.1 prepare takes an internal creation lock; postprocess releases it. Auto-released on failure. 2.2.3 prepare/postprocess support the with statement.

docs.title: CPython slot caveats
docs.text:
• CPython may change tp_getattro, tp_setattro, and related slots when you change __getattribute__, __setattr__, etc. If you are concerned, use ensure_type (or ensure_metaclass) to reset those slots, and avoid setting those dunder methods on private-attribute classes directly.
  • register_metaclass must be called with a metaclass that supports weakrefs.
  • Do not set __static_attributes__ on a private-attribute class — it will be removed.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class BankAccount(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_balance"]

    def __init__(self, balance):
        self._balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self._balance += amount      # ✅ accessible inside the class

    @property
    def balance(self):
        return self._balance

acct = BankAccount(100)
print(acct.balance)     # 100
acct.deposit(50)
print(acct.balance)     # 150

print(hasattr(acct, "_balance"))   # False — truly hidden
print(acct._balance)               # AttributeError: private attribute

docs.title: The three ingredients
docs.text:
1. Inherit PrivateAttrBase.
  2. Declare the private names in __private_attrs__.
  3. Use them normally inside the class — they're hidden everywhere else.
from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class MyClass(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["a", "b", "c"]   # a string, or a sequence of strings

    def __init__(self):
        self.a = 1
        self.b = 2
        self.c = 3

    def show(self):
        print(self.a, self.b, self.c)     # visible inside

obj = MyClass()
obj.show()                                # 1 2 3

print(hasattr(obj, "a"))                  # False
print(hasattr(obj, "b"))                  # False
print(hasattr(obj, "c"))                  # False

docs.title: What can be private?
docs.text:
• Instance attributes — the common case above.
  • Class attributes — usable from @classmethod.
  • Methods — declare the method's name in __private_attrs__ and it can only be called from the class's own code.
from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class Counter(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_count", "_increment"]

    _count = 0                            # class-level private state

    def _increment(self):                 # private method
        return 1

    def tick(self):
        self._count += self._increment()  # both accessible inside

    @classmethod
    def get_count(cls):
        return cls._count

c = Counter()
c.tick()
print(c.get_count())     # 1
print(hasattr(c, "_count"))       # False
print(hasattr(c, "_increment"))   # False

Next: learn about declaring attributes, or see the full API reference.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text:
This section explains the core concepts of private_attribute in depth.

  • Declaring private attributes — the basics of __private_attrs__.
  • Custom name generation — control how private values are stored with private_func.
  • Decorated methods — make arbitrary decorators work with PrivateWrapProxy.
  • Inheritance & use_parents — how privacy interacts with subclassing.

docs.title: Custom name generation
docs.text:
By default, private values are stored under generated hash names. You can control how the storage name is derived by supplying a private_func callable. It receives the object id and the attribute name:

def my_generate_func(obj_id: int, attr_name: str) -> str:
    return f"_hidden_{obj_id}_{attr_name}"

docs.title: Passing private_func
docs.text:
There are two equivalent ways to attach it:

from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

def my_generate_func(obj_id, attr_name):
    return f"_hidden_{obj_id}_{attr_name}"

# Option A: keyword in the class definition
class MyClass(PrivateAttrBase, private_func=my_generate_func):
    __private_attrs__ = ["secret"]

    def __init__(self):
        self.secret = 42

    def read(self):
        return self.secret

# Option B: on the base class itself
class Base(PrivateAttrBase, private_func=my_generate_func):
    ...

class MyClass(Base):
    __private_attrs__ = ["secret"]

Either way, private_func is optional; the default generates a tuple of two SHA-256 hashes.

Keep a strong reference

The metaclass stores a reference to private_func, so a local function used only for one class is safe to drop afterwards — the module handles its lifetime correctly (a past bug here caused a segfault on gc.collect(), now fixed). Still, for clarity prefer module-level functions.

docs.title: Declaring private attributes
docs.text:
List the private names in the __private_attrs__ class attribute. It accepts a single string or a sequence of strings.

from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class MyClass(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["a", "b", "c"]

    def __init__(self):
        self.a = 1
        self.b = 2
        self.c = 3

    def show(self):
        print(self.a, self.b, self.c)   # (1, 2, 3)

obj = MyClass()
obj.show()                              # 1 2 3

print(hasattr(obj, "a"))                # False
print(hasattr(obj, "b"))                # False
print(hasattr(obj, "c"))                # False

docs.title: What happens under the hood
docs.text:
When a name is declared private:

  1. Its value is not stored in the instance's __dict__.
  2. It is stored under a generated, collision-resistant name — by default a tuple of two SHA-256 hashes.
  3. Reads and writes are intercepted by tp_getattro / tp_setattro and routed to the private storage only when the accessing code belongs to the declaring class.

This is why the attribute is invisible to hasattr(), getattr(), and dir() from outside — the value simply isn't under the public name.

docs.title: Class-level private state
docs.text:
Private attributes can live on the class itself, which is useful with @classmethod:

from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class Config(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_api_key"]

    _api_key = "secret"

    @classmethod
    def get_key(cls):
        return cls._api_key

print(Config.get_key())        # secret
print(Config._api_key)         # AttributeError

docs.title: Private methods
docs.text:
Methods are attributes too. Declare a method's name and it becomes callable only from the declaring class's own code:

from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class Widget(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_secret_method", "_a"]

    def __init__(self, a):
        self._a = a

    def _secret_method(self):
        return self._a

    def public_method(self):
        return self._secret_method()

w = Widget(1)
print(w.public_method())       # 1
w._secret_method()             # AttributeError

docs.title: Interplay with __slots__
docs.text:
• Names declared in __slots__ cannot also appear in __private_attrs__.
  • However, when __slots__ is defined, private attributes may still be set inside methods — they live in the private-attribute storage, not in __dict__ or a slot.
from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class Slotted(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_secret"]
    __slots__ = ["public"]

    def __init__(self, secret, public):
        self._secret = secret    # OK — stored in private storage
        self.public = public

    def read(self):
        return self._secret

Note

The __private_attrs__ attribute itself is rewritten to a tuple of tuples after class creation, reflecting the generated storage names.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Decorators such as @lru_cache, @retry, or a custom wrapper return a new function object whose bytecode is not recognized as belonging to your class. Because private_attribute routes access by identifying which code object is doing the access, a plain wrapper would lose access to private attributes.

property, classmethod, and staticmethod are handled natively and need no special treatment. For everything else, wrap the decorator in PrivateWrapProxy.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase, PrivateWrapProxy

def deco(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

class MyClass(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["a", "b"]

    @PrivateWrapProxy(deco)
    def method1(self):
        return self.a

    @PrivateWrapProxy(deco)
    @PrivateWrapProxy(deco)
    def method2(self):
        return self.b

PrivateWrapProxy(decorator) returns a _PrivateWrap object that wraps the decorator application.

docs.title: .result and .funcs
docs.text:
The _PrivateWrap object exposes two public attributes:

Attribute Meaning .result The final decorated result. .funcs A read-only list proxy (_listproxy) of the original (pre-decoration) functions.

It is also transparent: it forwards __getattr__, __call__, and the descriptor __get__ to .result, so callers interact with the wrapped method as if it were the plain decorated function.

docs.title: Stacking, ordering, and name conflicts
docs.text:
To stack multiple decorators, resolve name conflicts, or fix decorator ordering, chain .result.<attr> onto the wrapped method and pass the method itself as the second argument. That second argument saves the previously captured functions:

from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase, PrivateWrapProxy

class MyClass(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["a", "b", "c"]

    @PrivateWrapProxy(deco1)
    def method1(self):
        return self.a

    @PrivateWrapProxy(method1.result.name1, method1)
    @PrivateWrapProxy(method1.result.name2, method1)
    def method1(self):        # final implementation; earlier ones are preserved
        return self.b

    @PrivateWrapProxy(deco2)
    def method2(self):
        return self.c

Here's how to read it:

  • Each @PrivateWrapProxy(method1.result.xxx, method1) line takes the method as currently built (method1), re-wraps it, and exposes the result under a new name (xxx) on method1.result.
  • The final def method1 is the "real" implementation.
  • Because each decoration layer saves the previous function, none of the earlier definitions are lost.

Warning

Do not pass PrivateWrapProxy a decorator that itself returns a _PrivateWrap — this raises TypeError.

docs.title: Inheritance & use_parents
docs.text: Private attributes follow strict per-declaring-class ownership rules. This is what gives them real privacy, but it also means you need to understand how they behave across an inheritance hierarchy.

docs.title: Subclasses cannot see parent privacy
docs.text:
Since v2.1.0, the code of a subclass cannot read or write a parent's private attribute. A parent's private attribute is reachable only from:

  • the parent's own code, or
  • a class that re-declares the same name in its own __private_attrs__.
from private_attribute import PrivateAttrBase

class Parent(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_secret"]

    def __init__(self):
        self._secret = 1

    def get_secret(self):
        return self._secret

class Child(Parent):
    __private_attrs__ = []

    def read_parent_secret(self):
        return self._secret   # AttributeError

obj = Child()
obj.get_secret()              # 1  — parent code sees parent value

docs.title: Re-declaring the same name
docs.text:
When a subclass re-declares a name in its own __private_attrs__, the two are stored separately — instance attributes per declaring class, class-level attributes per class. The parent's value is never overwritten by the child.

class Child(Parent):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_secret"]

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._secret = 99     # stored in Child's own storage

    def read_own(self):
        return self._secret

obj = Child()
obj.get_secret()    # 1  — parent code sees the parent's value
obj.read_own()      # 99 — child code sees its own value

docs.title: use_parents=True
docs.text:
Since v2.2.0, you can opt in to merging every ancestor's private names into the subclass's own set with use_parents=True:

class Parent(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_secret"]

    def __init__(self):
        self._secret = 1

    def get_secret(self):
        return self._secret

class Child(Parent, use_parents=True):
    __private_attrs__ = []

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._secret = 99      # stored in Child's own storage

    def read_own(self):
        return self._secret

obj = Child()
obj.get_secret()   # 1  — parent code sees the parent's value
obj.read_own()     # 99 — child code sees its own value

Key points:

  • The subclass's code may now read/write the parent's private names, but the values live in the subclass's own storage — they never overwrite the parent's own values.
  • The Python-level __private_attrs__ tuple is left unchanged; only the internal private-attribute name set is merged.
  • Default is False.

docs.title: Namespace restriction (v2.2.0)
docs.text:
A subclass must not define, in its own class body, a name that is private to a parent — unless it declares that name in its own __private_attrs__ or opts in with use_parents=True:

class Parent(PrivateAttrBase):
    __private_attrs__ = ["_secret"]

class Bad(Parent):              # TypeError
    __private_attrs__ = []
    _secret = 999

class Good(Parent, use_parents=True):
    __private_attrs__ = []
    _secret = 999               # OK — stored in Good's own storage

docs.title: Summary table
docs.text: Version Behavior ≤ 2.0 Subclasses could access parent private attributes. 2.1.0 Subclass code cannot access parent private attributes; re-declaring stores separately. 2.2.0 Namespace restriction on parent-private names; use_parents added.
